extracted.intended_audience: NaNoWriMo participants and novel writers seeking motivation and drafting advice
extracted.subtask_description: Motivational guidance for novelists taking part in NaNoWriMo (or drafting a first novel), focused on getting through the difficult middle, maintaining daily writing habits, and using concrete word-count goals and community pep talks to persevere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the next word
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the next word. Write it down. Repeat. Repeat. Repeat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neil Gaiman's concise imperative: focus on incremental progress — one word at a time — rather than grand plans. The repetition underscores persistence and the simple habit of continuing to put words on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist through the 'Great Swampy Middle'
rubrics_metrics.description: You’re past that first fine furious rapture... You’re in the middle, a little past the half-way point. The glamour has faded, the magic has gone... Welcome to the club. That’s how novels get written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the predictable slump in the middle of a novel and treat it as a normal part of the process. Expect dwindling enthusiasm, physical discomfort, and social friction; accepting this as 'the club' helps you keep going rather than quitting when the initial excitement fades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write despite fatigue and competing obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: finish my daytime work and THEN sit and write for another two or three hours for NaNoWriMo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make an explicit commitment to carve out writing time even after regular work. Discipline and time-management (scheduling writing sessions after daytime responsibilities) are presented as practical necessities for reaching NaNoWriMo goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain identity-based commitment: 'Writers write.'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because I'm a writer. And writers write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the self-definition of being a writer as motivation to act: see writing as central to your identity so that continuing to write becomes the expected behavior rather than something optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept imperfection in the first draft; prioritize finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t know why you started your novel... you’re pretty sure that even if you finish it it won’t have been worth the time... it would be a mercy simply to delete the whole thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combat paralyzing self-criticism by recognizing that first drafts rarely match the imagined ideal. The advice implies prioritizing completion over perfection and resisting the impulse to delete or abandon the manuscript because it 'falls short' of an internalized standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pep talks and community resources for motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: I would encourage you to read Neil Gaiman's entire article... Neil Gaiman is just one of dozens of authors who have written pep talks for NaNoWriMo. You can find them in the NaNoWriMo Pep Talk Archive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage external encouragement — essays, pep talks, and archives of advice from established authors — to renew motivation and normalize struggles. Seeking others' accounts of the writing process provides morale and practical perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set concrete, measurable word-count goals
rubrics_metrics.description: My word count right now is 13,952 and I plan to bring that up to 16,000 by the end of the day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific numeric targets to structure progress and create short-term, attainable milestones. Tracking and publishing (or noting) daily/period goals helps maintain momentum and gives a clear metric for success during NaNoWriMo.
